r0.why: Iron pyrite, iron sulfide FeS2 [1], most abundant sulfide mineral [2], luster and pale brass-yellow hue giving superficial resemblance to gold and the nickname [3].

r1.why: Associated sulfides or oxides, quartz veins, sedimentary and metamorphic rock, coal beds, replacement in fossils [5], small quantities of actual gold [6], invisible gold [7], controversial as of 1997 [9].

r2.why: Greek name from fire [10], ~400,000-year Suffolk Neanderthal site with burnt soil, fire-cracked handaxes and two pyrite fragments [13], Otzi's dates and fire kit [14].

r3.why: Copperas since classical times [16], heaped and weathered [17], runoff boiled with iron [18], 15th-century leaching replacing burnt sulfur [19], dominant by 19th century [20], sulfur dioxide, paper industry and sulfuric acid today [28].

r4.why: Brief 16th-17th century firearm use and wheellock with circular file [23], marcasite jewelry of small faceted pyrite often in silver since ancient times [21], radio mineral detector and hobbyists [24].

r5.why: Cathode in Energizer non-rechargeable lithium metal batteries [30], semiconductor [31], proposed for low-cost solar panels due to high visible-light absorption [33], all-pyrite thin-film cells [35].
